steps.say: The NIH prostatitis classification is applied to every case. Categories from Category I to IV are assigned by features. Category I and II are proven bacterial infections. Category III is divided into inflammatory and non inflammatory pain. Category IV is silent inflammation without symptoms. Treatment is matched to the assigned box.
steps.tx: The **NIH prostatitis classification** (four box system) sorts patients into **Category I to IV** (one to four): I for sudden bacterial attacks, II for lingering bacterial persistence, III for pelvic ache with IIIA inflammatory and IIIB non inflammatory flavours, and IV for silent inflammation. Classify first, because each box takes different drugs.

steps.say: Acute bacterial prostatitis is recognised clinically by abrupt fever. High temperature with marked perineal pain is considered typical. Severe voiding symptoms are reported together with retention. Vigorous rectal examination is avoided absolutely strictly in every case. Bacteria are showered widely into blood by massage. Urosepsis is precipitated rapidly by rough handling.
steps.tx: **Acute bacterial prostatitis** (sudden prostate infection, Category I (septic prostate)) strikes with high fever, perineal pain, and severe voiding symptoms; **avoid vigorous DRE** (no hard prostate squeeze), because massage showers bacteria into blood and triggers urosepsis. Start broad antibiotics after cultures without delay.

vis.alt: Prostatic ductal reflux with suppurative inflammation and swelling.
vis.caption: Acute bacterial infection refluxes into ducts: never massage vigorously. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Urinary retention is managed carefully without urethral instrumentation. Urethral catheterisation is avoided strictly in acute prostatitis. Suprapubic decompression is performed with a fine catheter. Ultrasound guidance is used routinely for safe placement. The line is left in place until normal flow returns. Bacteraemia is prevented reliably by this route.
steps.tx: In retention from acute prostatitis, **avoid urethral catheter** (no tube through the gland) and drain by fine **suprapubic decompression** (belly needle), because urethral instrumentation seeds bacteraemia. Place the suprapubic line under ultrasound and leave it till flow returns. Remove it promptly once voiding resumes spontaneously.

vis.alt: DRE technique with normal, BPH, cancer and prostatitis findings.
vis.caption: Prostatitis findings on DRE: examine gently, drain suprapubically. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Chronic bacterial prostatitis is treated patiently with prolonged antibiotics. Fluoroquinolones are prescribed specifically for tissue penetration. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg is given strictly twice daily. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is used as an alternative. Four to 6 weeks of continuous therapy is completed. The lipid barrier is crossed reliably by extended dosing.
steps.tx: **Chronic bacterial prostatitis** (lingering prostate infection, Category II (stubborn germs)) needs **fluoroquinolones** (penetrating antibiotics): ciprofloxacin **500 mg** (five hundred) twice daily, else trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole), continued **4 to 6 weeks** (four to six) to breach the **prostatic lipid barrier** (oily germ shield). Treat long enough, because short courses relapse.

steps.say: The Meares-Stamey test is ordered carefully for localisation. VB1 and VB2 urines are collected cleanly before massage. Expressed secretions are obtained gently by prostate massage. VB3 urine is collected promptly after massage. Bacterial counts are compared across the four glasses. Skin contamination is recognised carefully as a confounder.
steps.tx: The **Meares-Stamey test** (localisation cultures, **four-glass test** (four pot test)) sequences VB1 first void, then VB2 midstream, then **EPS** (expressed prostate fluid) squeezed by massage, ending with VB3 post massage urine, read by counts and microscopy. Localise before labelling chronic, because skin contaminants mimic infection.

steps.say: Prostatic abscess is suspected early with persistent swinging fever. Diabetics and immunocompromised hosts are affected most often. Multilocular fluid is demonstrated clearly on TRUS or CT. TRUS diagnosis is confirmed by urology review. Walled pus is recognised clearly as needing drainage. Rupture is prevented reliably by timely aspiration.
steps.tx: **Prostatic abscess** (prostate pus pocket) complicates uncontrolled infection in diabetics and the immunocompromised, diagnosed by **TRUS diagnosis** (rectal ultrasound) or CT showing multilocular fluid. Suspect it with swinging fever despite antibiotics, because walled pus needs drainage. Aspirate under cover rather than waiting for rupture.

steps.say: Abscess aspiration is performed promptly for sizeable fluctuant collections. Ultrasound guidance is used routinely for needle placement. Transurethral unroofing is selected wisely for midline cavities. Antibiotics are continued steadily alongside any surgical drainage. Re-imaging is arranged routinely after the procedure. Second passes are scheduled promptly for residual locules.
steps.tx: Drain abscesses over **1.5 cm to 2 cm** (one five to two) by **abscess aspiration** (needle suck) under ultrasound guidance or **transurethral unroofing** (roof removal) through TURP, keeping antibiotics alongside. Re-image after drainage, because residual locules need a second pass.

steps.say: Urethral caruncle is recognised as a benign meatal polyp. Painful bleeding is reported commonly by affected women. The posterior lip is the classic anatomical site. Topical estrogen is applied first as initial treatment. Excision is reserved strictly for refractory lesions. Biopsy is performed promptly when appearance is atypical.
steps.tx: **Urethral caruncle** (meatal berry) is a painful bleeding benign vascular polyp of the posterior lip in women, calmed first by **topical estrogen** (local hormone cream) before excision. Distinguish it from carcinoma by biopsy when atypical, because cancers mimic it. Reassure once histology confirms benign tissue.
